theme: Partiality; faith without works is dead
readingInstruction: Read James 2:1-26. This chapter has two parts: a warning against favoring the rich, and a famous argument that faith without works is dead. As you read, ask what kind of faith James is rejecting, and keep the whole chapter in view.
settingTheScene: In the first-century world, wealth bought honor, and the poor were treated as nobodies. James knew congregations where a rich man in fine clothing would be given a seat of honor while a poor man was told to stand or sit on the floor. This betrayed the gospel. The second half of the chapter takes on a different danger, a faith that is claimed but never lived. The question is not whether faith or works saves, but what kind of faith is real.
observation: “My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory” (v. 1).
“Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom?” (v. 5).
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 8).
“What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?” (v. 14).
“So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (v. 17).
“For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead” (v. 26).
interpretation:
James begins with a clear principle: “show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.” The church is where the world’s rankings are overturned. If you honor the rich man and dishonor the poor, you have “become judges with evil thoughts.” God has chosen the poor to be “rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom,” and yet they were the ones being insulted, while the rich were the ones oppressing the church and blaspheming the name. The “royal law” is to love your neighbor as yourself. To show partiality is to be “convicted by the law as transgressors,” for whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become accountable for all of it. We will be judged by “the law of liberty,” so speak and act accordingly. “For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.”

The second half asks a pointed question: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?” The Greek makes clear that the answer is no: that kind of faith cannot save. James gives an example. If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking daily food, and you say, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving what is needed, what good is that? “So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.” It is not merely weak; it is dead. Next James imagines an objector who says that one has faith and another has works. James replies, “Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works.” Then he points out that even the demons believe that God is one, and shudder. Mere agreement with a fact is not saving faith.

Two examples follow. Abraham was “justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar.” James says that “faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works; and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” Rahab the prostitute was also “justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way.” James concludes: “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.”

How does this fit with Paul, who says in Romans 4 that Abraham was justified by faith apart from works? Most Reformed and evangelical interpreters answer that Paul and James are fighting different enemies. Paul argues against those who say works earn salvation. James argues against those who say that a profession without obedience is enough. Paul uses “justify” to mean being declared righteous before God, while James uses it to mean being shown to be righteous, vindicated by what one does. Paul says we are saved by faith alone; James says the faith that saves is never alone. Both agree that real faith produces obedience. We explore this on Day 839.
connection: Leviticus 19:18 is the source of the royal law, and Jesus affirmed it in Matthew 22:39. Deuteronomy 1:17 forbids partiality in judgment. 1 Corinthians 1:26-29 says God chose the weak and low. Matthew 25:31-46 ties judgment to mercy shown to the needy. 1 John 3:17-18 echoes James on love in deed. Genesis 15:6 and Romans 4:1-5 are the texts about Abraham’s faith. Genesis 22 is the offering of Isaac. Joshua 2 and Hebrews 11:31 are about Rahab. Ephesians 2:8-10 joins grace and good works.
application:
Ask yourself whom you tend to favor and whom you tend to overlook, whether at church, at work, or among your neighbors. Treat one overlooked person with real honor this week.

Meet a concrete need today, for someone near you, with more than good wishes.

Memorize verse 13 as a reminder: mercy triumphs over judgment.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have favored the wealthy or the powerful.
Ask God to show you the faith that works through love.
Thank him that he chose the poor to be rich in faith.
